†*281. PROF M.M. AG ARWAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn towards the news-
item published in Hmdustan of 23rd December, 2001 under the caption, "Prati 
varsh paanch bazar krishi klinic kholne ka faisla"; 
(b) if so, the details of the proposal; 
(c) whether Government would also provide agriculture related training 
to farmers through these clinics; and 
(d) if so, by when the said clinics would start functioning in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (d)A new Scheme "Establishment of Agri-clinics andAgri-business 
Centres" has recently been launched in collaboration with National Bank for 
Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). The scheme proposes to assist 
agriculture graduates and graduates in subjects allied to agriculture in setting 
up of around 5,000 Agri-clinics/Agri-business ventures per year in identified 
activities through Bank finance with refinance from NABARD on self 
employment basis. Start up training of two to three months in the areas of 
entrepreneurship and business management as well as for skill improvement in 
the chosen area of activity will also be provided to agricultural graduates 
interested in setting up agri-clinics and agri-business veniures. Graduates who 
propose to avail the benefit of the Scheme will be given bank finance on 
priority sector lending terms on acceptance of their project proposals. The 
average cost of an individual venture is estimated to be around Rs. 5 lakhs,

the management thinks that an employee is required in a steel plant, it may not 
allow the employee to go on voluntary retirement. It is not compulsory on the 
part of the management to agree to employees' equest for voluntary retirement. 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Sir, so many employees have accepted this 
scheme. Many employees are waiting to get relief and the benefits. Is there any 
mechanism that has been evolved to give quick relief and benefits to the 
employees? 
SHRI BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY: Sir, as I have already said, the 
manpower in SAIL has become surplus mainly becuase of changes in technology, 
high skill requirement, skill obsolescence, process improvement, competitive 
requirements, work flexibility and low turnover. This is the main reason why 
VRS has been introduced in SAIL, and it is working properly. It started in 1998-
99; and for two years, that is, in 1998-99 and 1999-2000. it was a different 
scheme. Now, another scheme has been introduced since 2001-2002. The new 
scheme has already been introduced and it is helping the employees. 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Sir, the hon. Minister has stated 
in his reply that 26,122 workers have taken VRS. The SAIL has to pay around 
Rs. 1000 crores towards their dues. If SAIL has paid this amount of Rs. 1000 
crores, I want to know the benefits that it has derived. How much money SAIL 
has saved by giving VRS to these employees? The second part of my question 
is this. The reforms started in the year 1991. Everybody has been saying that 
they have surplus manpower and that rights izing of manpower is required. But, 
from 1991 to 2002, thousands of workers, both executives and non-executives, 
have been appointed in SAIL, and some of them have been appointed without 
any interviews. If it is so, what is the number of workers that have been appointed 
from 1991 to 2002? 
SHRI BRAJ KISHORETRIPATHY: Sir, VRS has been introduced. SAIL 
has the objective of rightsizing its manpower. But it is mainly because of the 
mechanisation activities that are going on, and the modernisation activities 
that are going on in SAIL. So, for meeting the requirements of their steel plants, 
the SAIL is having its own recruitment programme, So, recruitment has been 
going on. But it is being done on a very limited scale. Whenever it is necessary, 
from the point of view of technical upgradation, etc., they are doing recruitment; 
but it is not being done, in a general sense. After modernisation, if the manpower 
is surplus in a certain department or in a unit, they are allowed to take voluntary 
retirement. If some new technical persons are needed, then the management 
recruits those people through a proper recruitment process. Sir, at the moment, I 
don't have the figures relating to new recruitment. If the hon. Member is so 
interested, I can give it to hitr; subsequently. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATI ACHARYA: Sir, my question is very simple. I want 
to know whether the voluntary retirement scheme is being introduced or is being 
vigorously pursued in the SAIL, by spending thousands of crores of rupees to 
facilitate the self-out of the SAIL, to reduce the liability of the promoter who will 
be taking over the SAIL in the days to come; or, for some other purpose. Would 
the hon. Minister clarify it? 
SHRI BRAJ KISHORETRIPATHY: Sir, I have already explained that the 
voluntary retirement scheme was introduced to reduce or rightsize the 
manpower. One of the factors responsible for the SAIL incurring loss was because 
its manpower was much more, in comparison to other steel plants in the world. 
At the moment, we are competing with different steel plants in the world market. 
Our labour cost is about 21 per cent compared to other new steel plants whose 
!6 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYASABHA 
labour cost is 2—4 per cent. It indicates that our labour cost is much more, 
compared to other steel plants. Therefore, in order to rightsize the manpower, 
the Voluntary Retirement Scheme was introduced. Initially, in 1998-1999 and 
in 1999-2000, this scheme was introduced, on deferred payment basis. Under 
that scheme, the SAIL had not incurred any cash flow because the employees 
were paid every month, on deferred payment basis. But, after that, in 1999-2000 
and 2000-2001, a new scheme, as per the DPE guidelines, was introduced. 
Under that scheme, the Govemment is giving guarantee a loan, to the extent of 
Rs. 1,500 crores, and the Govemment is also allowing an interest subsidy of 
50 per cent. That is why the SAIL has availed of this loan and is offering 
voluntary retirement to its employees. Sir, by 2003, the expected expenditure 
on this would be about Rs. 1,000 crores.

Flood damage in Kerala  
*286. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have extended special assistance towards 
flood damage caused due to South-West Monsoon, set in Kerala on 25th May, 
2001; 
17

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
(b) the estimated damage in different sectors due to the flood havoc; 
(c) the magnitude of damage assessed by the Central Team; 
(d) whether Government released the assistance recommended by the 
Central Team; 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(0 whether Government would consider releasing financial assistance 
recommended therein? 
THE MINISTER OF. AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (0 A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (0 Following heavy rains on 8th and 9th July, 2001, a number of 
districts including Kannur, Idukki, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and 
Ernakulum were affected by floods. 
According to the State Government, 119 human lives were lost, 1352 
villages were affected, resulting in evacuation of 35,000 people. Around 1700 
bunds were damaged, cropped area of 0.40 lakh hectares was affected. Damage 
was also reported to a number of Highways and Roads. 
Services of Armed Forces and Central Para-Military Forces were made 
available to assist in search and rescue operations. A Central Team was deputed 
to assess the extent of damage and assistance required. The amount found 
admissible as per the prescribed items and rates of assistance from the National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) were within the available balances of the 
Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) of the State. The High Level Committee of 
Ministers, accordingly, did not approve any allocation from the NCCF. 
A sum of Rs. 26.47 crores was released to the State as advance Central 
Share of its CRF. Allocation of 5,000 MTs of rice was made available free of cost. 
No further assistance to the State Government is due for these floods as 
there are still adequate balances in its CRF. 
SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: Sir, in the last monsoon season in Kerala, 
the rains caused heavy damages. I remember, a Central team was deputed by the 
Govemment of India to look into it and assess the damage. The Central team has 
submitted its report to the Government of India, but, so far, no relief has been 
given to the State of Kerala which suffered huge damages. Sir, it is to be noted 
18 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYASABHA 
that the then Agriculture Minister, Nitish Kumarji, is sitting here. He visited the State 
of Kerala and had a meeting with the Chief Minister, the Ministers and the M.Ps from 
Kerala there. He had assured that something would be done after looking into the 
case. Subsequently, the Chief Minister, the Revenue Minister and all the M.Rs from 
Kerala had a meeting with the present Agriculture Minister, and he had assured that 
adequate relief would be given to the State of Kerala so as to compensate the State. 
The answer which he has given to us is, the National Calamity Contingency 
Fund, NCCF, and the Calamity Relief Fund, CRF, were being compared. Funds for 
Kerala have been allocated under the Calamity Relief Fund. The reason for the non-
allocation of funds from the NCCF has been that since there is adequate Calamity 
Relief Fund with the State, there no further assistance due to the State. 
My first supplementary to the hon. Minister is this: The CRF that had been 
given to Kerala has already been exhausted. An assurance was given to the 
Revenue Minister that when the CRF is exhausted, the position would be reviewed 
and assistance would be given. If that be the case, I would like to know whether 
the Minister would clarify the postition with regard to the further assistance to 
Kerala, when the CRF is exhausted. 
SHRI AJIT SINGH: A Central team visited Kerala, and their 
recommendation is that there are enough funds available with the State. 
According to the norms laid down for National Calamity Contingency Fund, 
all the fund under the CRF should be exhausted first; but, here, the fund is 
still'available with the State. It has not been spent and, hence, there is no need 
to release further funds from the Contingency Fund. 
SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: My specific point was whether the 
CRF has been exhausted. To my limited knowledge, the CRF has been 
exhausted in the State. If the CRF has been exhausted, I would like to know 
whether further assistance would be allowed. 
SHRI AJIT SINGH: The Calamity Relief Fund is provided for certain type 
of problems that occur because of a calamity. Norms for the release of funds 
from the National Calamity Contingency Fund are laid down. If the CRF money 
is spent, then the money would be given from the National Calamity 
Contingency Fund. It is true. But our committee report states that there are 
enough funds available with the State. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: During the same monsoon season, 
relief from NCCF was given to so many other States, like Orissa, Gujarat. If 
that were the case, the non-allocation of funds from NCCF to the State of 
Kerala is a discriminatory approach on the part of the Centre towards the 
State of Kerala. 
SHRI AJIT SINGH: Funds from the NCCF are allocated after teams are 
sent to the States. The group of Ministers meets, and, on the basis of the

discrimination against Kerala or any other State, for that matter. Very strict 
norms have been laid down as to what kind of expenses are allowed under the 
National Calamity Contingency Fund. Reconstruction work is not really 
allowed. According to the Eleventh Finance Commission's report, the damage 
caused to the infrastructure is riot allowed under the National Calamity 
Contingency Fund; that would be met from the Plan expenditure*.

life and forestry should be declared as priority sector for which funds should be

Statement 
Wildlife Conservation Strategy 
The details of the Wildlife Conservation Strategy-2002 adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife are—  
1. Wildlife and forests shall be declared priority sector at the national level 
for which funds should be earmarked. 
2. Law enforcement agencies must ensure that those engaged in poaching, illicit 
trade in wildlife and wild life products, destruction of their habitat, and such 
other illegal activities are given quick and deterrent punishment. 
3. We should fully tap the potential in wildlife tourism and at the same time 
take care that it does not have adverse impact in wildlife and protected 
areas. The revenue earned from increased tourism should be used entirely to 
augment available resources for conservation. 
4. Protecting interests of the poor and tribals living around protected areas should 
be handled with sensitivity and with maximum participation of the affected 
people. They should have access to the minor forest produce, in the forest 
outside of national parks and sanctuaries. Employment and means generation 
for these people is crucial for maintaining symbiosis between the forests, 
wildlife and the people. People should be encouraged to take up 
afforestation and conservation in new areas. 
74 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
5. While strengthening protective measures against traditional threats to 
wildlife, we should also respond to newer threats such as toxic chemicals and 
pesticides. 
6. There should be greater governmental as well as societal recognition and 
support for the'many non-governmental organizations engaged in wildlife 
conservation. Mainstream media to better highlight their activities as also 
successes of governmental initiative that have worked. 
7. Creatively produced Television Programmes on wildlife and ecology are 
widely appreciated by young and old as seen from the popularity of 
dedicated T.V. channels like, Discovery, National Geographic and 
Animal Planet. It proposed that Prasar Bharati and other private channels along 
with agencies like WWF for Nature should collaborate and increase original 
Indian Content in different languages on our television. 
8. No diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes for critical and 
ecologically fragile wildlife habitat shall be allowed. 
9. Lands falling within 10 km. of the boundaries of National Parks and 
Sanctuaries should be notified as Eco-fragile zones under section 3(v) of 
the Environment (Protection) Act and Rule 5 Sub-rule S(viii) & (x) of the 
Environment (Protection) Rules. 
 
10. Removal of encroachments and illegal activities from within forestlands and 
Protected Areas. 
11. No commercial monoculture to replace natural forests. 
12. The settlement of rights in National Parks and Sanctuaries should not be 
used to exclude or reduce the areas that are crucial and integral part of the 
wildlife habitat. 
13. More than 2000 vacant posts in the frontline staff of Protected Areas shall 
be filled immediately and provided basic infrastructure for efficient discharge 
of duties. Ban on recruitment of staff against vacant post should be lifted 
on lines with the Police Department. Innovative initiative such as 
redeployment of surplus employees in other departments, hiring local 
people on voluntary or honorarium basis, raising donations from business 
houses and other members of the public in return for a greater role for them in 
implementing programmes need to be explored. 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
14. Every protected area should be managed by forest officers trained in 
wildlife management. 
15. Mitigation measures for human-animal conflict and mechanism for crop 
insurance, as also expeditious disbursements of ex-gratia payments 
should be instituted by States. 
16. Forest Commission should be set-up to look into restructuring, reform 
and strengthening the entire forest set up and affiliated institutions in 
the country. 
17. A working group Shall be constituted to monitor implementation of 
Wildlife Action Plan.

Central Pollution Control Board.

in cluster of small scale industrial units has been taken up. 91 CETP 
projects have been taken up.

DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SMT.) RITA VERMA): (a) to (e) The Government is

Statement-Il 
Details of schemes for empowerment of women 
1. Women Component Plan 
The Ninth Five Year Plan has adopted the concept of the Women 
Component Plan under which at least 30% of funds/benefits of concerned 
Departments/Ministries are to be earmarked for women. 
2. Rural Women's Development and Empowerment Project 
(Swa-Shakti):— The Swa-Shakti Project, earlier known as Rural Women's 
Development and Empowerment Project, was sanctioned on 16-10-1998 as a 
Centrally-sponsored Project for a period of 5 years with an estimated outlay of 
Rs. 186.21 crore. In addition, an amount of Rs. 5 crore is being provided during 
the project period, for facilitating the setting up, in the project States, of 
Revolving Funds for giving interest-bearing loans to beneficiary groups 
primarily during their initial formative stage. 
3. Integrated Women's Empowerment Programme (Swayamsidha) 
Swayamsidha is an Integrated scheme for Women's empowerment. It is 
based on formation of women into Self-Help groups (SHGs) and aims at holistic 
empowerment of women through awareness generation, economic empowerment 
and convergence of various schemes. 
110 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The vision of Swayamsidha is to mobilize and develop empowered 
women who will: 
• Demand their rights from family, community and government. 
• Have increased access to an control over, material, social and political 
resources; 
 
• Have enhanced awareness and improved skills; and 
• Be able to raise issues of common concern through mobilization and 
networking. 
4. Women in Difficult Circumstances (Swadhar): 
The schemes has been designed with a flexible and innovative approach 
to cater to the requirement of various types of women in distress in diverse 
situations under different conditions. The scheme provides shelter, counselling 
and training for women in difficult circumstances who do not have any social 
and economic support. 
5. Awareness Generation Projects for Rural & Poor Women: 
The Awareness Generation Programme aims to identify the needs of rural 
and poor women and to generate awareness among them about their status in 
the family and society and to activate them to work for achieving their rights 
and to deal with social issues. Since 1993-94, special emphasis has been given 
to participation of women in Panchayati Raj institutions and their role in 
promoting national integration and communal harmony. 
6. Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP) 
This programme launched in 1987, seeks to provide updated skills and 
new knowledge to poor and assetlcss women in the traditional sectors, such as 
agriculture, animal husbandry, dairying, fisheries, handlooms, handicrafts, khadi 
and village industries, sericulture, social forestry and wasteland development 
for enhancing their productivity and income generation. This would enhance 
and broaden their employment opportunities, including self-employment and 
development of entrepreneurial skills. 
7. Women's Economic Programme (NORAD) 
This programme was launched in 1982-83 with assistance from Norwegian 
Agency for Development Corporation (NORAD). Under this programme, 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
financial assistance is given to Women's Development Corporations, Public 
Sector Corporations, autonomous bodies and voluntary organisations to train 
poor women, mostly in non-traditional trades and to ensure their employment 
in these areas.

preventive action taken in respect thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE 1NTHE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) Trafficking is 
prevalent as a social evil in some families of Banchhra caste in Madhya Pradesh. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The Govemment of Madhya Pradesh has already been implementing a 
scheme called Jabali through voluntary organisations for taking up activities for 
the welfare and development of women and child victims of commercial sexual 
exploitation so as to eliminate commercial sexual exploitation. The scheme is 
mainly targeted at the women and children in those castes-7 tribes where there is 
social acceptance and even collusion by the male members with the commercial 
sexual exploitation of their women. The scheme has five components: 
(i)  running of Boarding Schools for children or women victims; 
(ii) setting up shelter / protective homes for young girls; 
(iii) providing women victims benefits for income generation and 
economic rehabilitation; 
(iv) creation of public awareness through information, education and 
publicity; and 
(v) health check ups and treatment. 
At present 6 voluntary organisations in the State are engaged in running 
shelter/protective homes providing facilities to 500 children. In addition the 
State Government has formulated a Plan of Action with the objective to 
mainstream and reintegrate the victims of commercial sexual exploitation 
through strategies grouped under awareness generation and social mobilisation, 
health care services including HIV AIDS, education alternative education system 
through ashrams, etc. 
116 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The details of AIDS afflicted women caste-wise are not maintained. 
However, the total number of AIDS patients including men and women in the 
State of Madhya Pradesh as on 28.2.2002 is 759. Govemment has launched a 
comprehensive AIDS prevention and control programme, which is a 100% 
centrally sponsored scheme being implemented in all States / UTs including 
Madhya Pradesh through States / UTs AIDS Control Societies. The main 
components of the Programme consist of: 
(i) reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification of 
target populations and providing counselling, condom promotion, 
and treatment of sexually transmitted infections; 
(ii) preventive intervention for the general population by information, 
education and communication (IEC) and awareness campaign, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, sale blood transfusion 
services and prevention of occupational exposure; 
(iii) providing financial assistance for opportunistic infections, home 
and community based care; 
(iv) strengthening effectiveness and technical, managerial financial 
sustainability at national, state and municipal levels; 
(v) promoting collaboration amongst public, private and coluntary 
sector.

Growth of Education 
2144. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of HUM AN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether growth of education in India at the primary level, has not 
been very spectacular; 
(b) whether growth at the secondary level has been even more erratic; 
118 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether, despite the growth in the number of institutes of higher 
learning, the total all India enrolment in graduate and higher level courses was only 
three percent of the total enrolments in 1998, and the data for 1990s shows a slow 
down in improvement in the education levels; 
(d) if the answer to parts (a) to (c) above be in the affirmative, the reasons 
therefor; and 
(e) the remedial steps contemplated by Govemment in this regard? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SMT.) RITA VERMA): (a) to (e) The growth of 
education at primary level has been significant Primary Schools have increased from 
2,10,000 in 1950-51 to 6,42,000 in 1999-2000; Upper Primary Schools from 
13,600 to 1,98,000; Enrolment in Primary from 19.2 million to 113.61 million and 
in Upper Primary from 3 million to 42 million. Similarly, there has been an increase 
from 7,416 institutions of High / Higher Secondary / Inter / Pre-Jr. Colleges in 
1950-51 to 1,16,820 in 1999-2000. The enrolment in High/ Hr. Sec. / Inter / Pre-
degree Schools has also increased from 19.1 million in 1990-91 to 27.76 million 
in 1998-99. Further, there had been continuous increase in student enrolment in 
higher education as well as the number of institutions providing higher education 
since independence. Enrolment in higher education was 49.25 lakhs in 1990-91 
which increased to 80.01 lakhs in 2000-2001 which shows 62.5% increase over the 
year 1990-91. Average annual increase in number of students in the last one decade 
i.e., since 1990-91 is 3.08 lakhs. The absolute increase in student enrolment per 
year during nineties is around 3 lakhs which does not show any kind of slow down. 
The Technical Education sector has also kept pace with the changing economy and 
there has been a steady growth in the sector. The intake capacity has increased over 
the years and new institutes have come in existence to meet the demands. The 
number of institutions for graduate courses has increased from 857 in 1997-98 to 
980 in 1998-99 and the intake capacity has increased from 1,49,479 to 1,71,180. 
Similarly, for post-graduate courses, the number of institutions has increased from 
1,022 in 1997-98 to 1,276 in 1998-99 whereas the intake capacity has 
increased from 75,956 to 84,524.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SMT.) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c)The goal 
of the National Literacy Mission (NLM) is to attain full literacy i.e. a sustainable

Rakesh Mohan Committee Report 
2172. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: 
SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the major recommendations of the Rakesh Mohan Committee 
Report on Indian Railways; 
(b) whether Govemment have since examined these recommendations; if 
so, the details thereof; 
(c) how far these have been taken care of in the Railway Budget 2002-
2003; and 
(d) the reasons for not fully implementing the recommendations 
of the Report and Government's reaction regarding their implementation? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
140 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
O. RAJAGOPAL):(a)The major recommendations of the Railway Expert Group 
headed by Dr. Rakesh Mohan are as under: 
1. Institutional separation of roles into policy, regulatory and management 
functions. This will mean: 
i. Policy makers are limited for setting policy (and paying for what 
they ask for). The Govemment of India will be in charge of setting 
policy direction. 
ii. Provide operational authonomy and insulate Indian Railways by 
corporatising it into "Indian Railways Corporations" (IRC). It would 
be governed by a reconstituted Indian Railways Executive Board. 
iii. Set up an Indian Rail Regulatory Authority to regulate IRC's 
activities as a monopoly supplier of rail services particularly 
related to tariff setting. 
2. Ex ante acceptance and commitment by the Govemment and Indian 
Railways that Indian Railways will operate on commercial lines are the necessary 
conditions for the reorganisation to be successful exercise. Non-commercial 
activities mandated by the government will be clearly demonstrated and Indian 
Railways appropriately compensated for such activities. 
3. In view of financial crisis Indian Railways to pursue the strategic High 
Growth pattern for financial recovery. 
 
4. Exemption from taxation—excise, sales tax etc. for the period of 
transition, say 5—7 years. 
5. Set up a Social Safety net to take care of surplus labour. 
6. Restructuring of financial accounts of Indian Railways in accordance with 
the Companies Act, 1956. 
7. Spinning off non-core activities. 
8. Rebalancing of tariffs to eliminate cross subsidisation. 
(b) to (d) A Committee of serior officers of Railway Board are examining the 
various recommendations and will be submitting its report soon. 
In the budget proposals 2002-03, a beginning has been made to rationalise the 
freight structure by removing existing anomalies that had crept up in the 
141 

RAJYASABHA [22 March, 2002] 
course of time. It has also been proposed to rationalise the passenger fares for 
proper tariff rebalancing by modifying the taper in the fare structure to remove 
the existing anomalies and making other marginal changes in respect of 
minimum fares and rationalising the relativity of fares of various classes. 
Impiementation of the recommendations of the Report will be on the 
basis of the recommendations of the Committee of senior officers of Railway 
Board.

contacted in case of emergency. The boarding station as well as the

or otherwise sick person travelling on concessional fare should carry

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND

of genome sequences of 3.2 billion bases and around 31,000 genes (14,000 
known and about 17,000 predicted genes) of human genome in February, 
2001 has ushered in challenges in relation to understanding of functions of 
these genes, and using these to develop medically beneficial products. The era 
of genomics has opened opportunities to discover new drug targets. This

industry and about 30 recombinant drugs are already in the market and about 
300—400 products are under clinical trials.

GOOD WISHES TO THE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today, we bid farewell to some of 
our fellow Members who will retire during this year on completion of their term. 
Some of the Members, who will be retiring in July and November this year, 
would perhaps feel that I am bidding them Good-bye too soon. While doing so, 
I am. only following a well-established convention developed, over the years, 
in this House. We have been customarily holding farewells during this part of 
the Session, as some of our colleagues may not be there, till the second part 
of the current Session. 
Those who are retiring will certainly be missed by the House. In 
particular, we shall miss those Members who always took prominent part in eur 
deliberations, and made the debate of this august House lively. In this House, 
we have shared our joys and sorrows. Members belonging to this House 
represent diversity of the nation.   Members may belong to the ruling 
196 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
party or the Opposition, but when they are in this House, they have a common 
goal, namely,. the development of the nation and the welfare of the people. 
Serving the people does not stop after one has ceased to be the 
Member of this House. Through this House, no doubt, you have served the 
nation, but after retiring from the membership of this House, you are getting 
yet another opportunity to help others. You may not have the burden of 
parliamentary work, but, I am sure, you would be getting more opportunities to 
reach out those who really need your help. The knowledge and experience 
acquired would stand them in good stead. 
Your membership of tne House invests you with an enviable ability to 
influence the legislative output. Your labours, when translated into laws, have 
impacted the lives of millions of people. I am sure that now, when you leave 
the House, it shall be with a sense of fulfilment at having played a part in the 
grand process of building of our nation. 
I take this opportunity to place on record my personal appreciation 
and thanks for the valuable contribution made by all retiring Members and the 
courtesy, consideration and cooperation extended by them to the Chair. I wish 
them good health, happiness and peaceful time while they serve the nation 
outside the House.

very long innings. Shri N.K.P. Salve, who was just sitting by my side, and who 
had long 24 years in this House; after 2nd of April, we will not be able to get 
him, he is retiring. Mr. Chavan, who has the distinction of being the Leader of 
the House, Leader of my Party, for a very long period of time, and, perhaps, a 
person who had the longest innings as Minister. My period of membership is a 
little less than his total period of Ministership in both the Central Government 
and the State Government put together. We would also be deprived of his rich 
experiences.   Mr. Sikander Bakht, who was the Leader of the House, and 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
the Leader of the Opposition, and always made very valuable contributions in 
conducting the proceedings of the House. We will be missing many of our very 
distinguished colleagues, but, at the same time, those who are continuing will 
remember their valuable contributions not only in framing legislations, 
articulating their views, representing the different sets of opinion, but also 
sometimes, occasionally, in representing the collective views. Sir, you have 
very correctly pointed out that this House is unique, in the sense that it is not a 
secondary Chamber, nor even the second Chamber; in fact, on some 
occasions, it is a Chamber which is enjoying the full powers, like the other 
Chamber, which is directly elected by the people, especially, in the areas of 
amendment of the Constitution, and certain special powers which the other 
House does not enjoy, like creating All-India Services, enabling Parliament to 
make legislations on the items enumerated in the State List, etc. 
Sir, this year is the 50th year of the establishment of the Rajya 
Sabha. We have covered half-a-century, and, perhaps, when we look back, in 
all humility and modesty, I would like to say that we can claim that this 
Chamber, the Council of States, the Rajya Sabha, has contributed, in its own 
way, to strengthen the democratic institution. No doubt, sometimes, to your 
irritation, to your annoyance, we quarrel among ourselves, create 
disturbances, sometimes, leading to the adjournment of the House, but, the 
moment we leave this Chamber and meet in the Lobby, we leave the 
temporary bitterness here itself, and we completely forget about those 
incidents. But, Sir, whenever the situation demands, as it happened just a 
couple of days back, the whole House, through the Leader of the House, 
expressed its opinion against the vandalism, against the attack on the 
legislative building. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, I entirely agree with you when you say that our 
retiring colleagues will no doubt make their contributions in various fields. 
Some of them are coming back, like my young friend, Shri Suresh Pachouri, 
who has already been re-elected, and you will be welcoming them; but, some 
of our colleagues who will not join us in the second leg of the Session will no 
doubt make their contributions to the welfare of the people and to the 
development of the nation. Yesterday, when Shri Adhik Shirodkar was 
conducting the proceedings of the House, I was witnessing the command that 
he exercised. Obviously, as a distinguished advocate and with his training and 
a judicial mind, he always guides the Members on how to conduct themselves. 
No doubt, we will be missing them. At the same time, I would like to say that 
after returning back to their respective

wishes and wish good health. I am not saying good-bye to them, but only 
wishing them good health.

SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, I, on behalf of my 
party, the RSP, extend my best wishes -- and best health -- to the retiring 
Members. This is the House of versatile personalities. Many eminent 
personalities amongst us are now retiring. But in politics, in public life and in 
social life, there is no retirement. The term 'retirement' is strange in political 
and social life. Therefore, I hope the Members, who are retiring for the time 
being from this House, will contribute still more, because the need of the hour 
is to render service to the nation and to the mankind. As far as our nation is 
concerned, an all round effort is required for building the 
204 

[22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
nation, for strengthening communal harmony and for our country's progress. I 
hope the retiring Members will be guiding us in future also, with their 
contribution, whether they are in Parliament or outside. Eminent personalities 
like Chavanji, Salveji, Sikander Bakhtji and Shirodkarji, who are our elders 
and very senior Members, are retiring. But there is an array of young 
Members like Shri P. N. Siva, Shri Soundararajan, Shri Subbian and Shri 
Peter Alphonse, who are also retiring from this House. Of course, it is 
inevitable. It is not because of age, but because of experience. I have had 
one-and-a-half years' experience of being in the Upper House, the Council of 
States. Before this, I had two-and-a-half years' experience of being a Member 
of the other House, the Lower House, in the Eleventh and the Twelfth Lok 
Sabha. 
I remember, even Mr. Siva was with me in the Eleventh Lok Sabha. 
He could not complete his term there. Both the Eleventh and Twelfth Lok 
Sabha could not complete their terms. I think Mr. Siva could not complete his 
term in the Rajya Sabha also. 1 hope he would also come back and render his 
eminent service in this Council of States. Sir, we have learnt a lot from our 
seniors during this short span of time. We are benefited by this experience. 
So, I assure the retiring Members, on behalf of my party and on behalf of the 
whole House, that their contribution will be remembered for ever by this House 
and the people of this country. Some retiring Members are coming back, it is 
good; those who are not able to come back, I hope, they would continue to 
contribute for the betterment of the nation. Sir, with these words, I, on behalf 
of my party, once again convey my best regards and wishes to the retiring 
Members.

of significance that has been given to me is science. It is clearly written. 
Therefore, I would like to compare this august House with what a group of 
scientists would have done. 
I notice that when there is a difference of opinion between two sides 
of the House, very rough words are exchanged; of course, within the 
Parliamentary restrictions, but they are very rough. At the same time, the

to be remembered, and a day that will remain in our minds for ever. Sir, when

life is not only a bed of roses, but also a bed of thorns. I had read in one of the 
poems, "We meet, we know, we love, only to part". This parting may not be 
permanent, but, of course, it has its own impact. If I may recall the farewell 
address that you gave in 2000, when I came here as a Member, you rightly 
said, "After you have become old, you will be narrating to your grandsons your

House, will have a special mention." In parliamentary term, you said, "We will 
have a Special Mention". I remember those words. I will be doing injustice if I 
start naming persons, who had impressed me, who had helped me, for, in the 
course of my speech, and in my emotional mood, I may leave out the name of 
one or the other person. So, I don't want to name any one, in particular. My 
thanks and gratitude goes to one and all here. First of all, Sir, I am grateful to 
my party, which bom 80 years ago, with the only objective of uplifting the 
suppressed, oppressed and the depressed classes of the society. 
But for my leader, Mr. Karunanidhi and Mr. Maran, one of the senior 
most Members in Parliament for having been here for more than 35 years, 
which has heightened me all through my tenure and my party, I could

hon. Members are waiting, as to when this will be over. That is why I do not

of fulfilment.  I am going with a great achievement. 
Sir, I worked with Smt. Indira Gandhi. I worked with Mr. Rajiv Gandhi, 
I also worked with Mr. P.V. Narasimha Rao. And, after being in the Opposition, 
I am, now, working with Smt. Sonia Gandhi. I am, particularly, grateful to all 
these leaders, because they have given me an opportunity of serving the 
country in different capacities. I have been in Parliament for almost twenty 
years and in the Maharashtra Assembly for almost 25 years. So, I must say 
that, while discharging my duties, there might have been occasions when I

particular cause, irrespective of who the person is, you have to discharge your 
duties consciously. 
I feel very proud when I am reminded of the work done in Punjab. Sir, 
Punjab was on the brink of anarchy and everybody was saying that there was 
hardly any possibility of holding elections in the State. I feel very happy that we 
could conduct elections there. We could bring the people of Punjab into the 
mainstream. I am not bothered whether the Congress Party was in power. 
Bringing the people of Punjab into the mainstream gave me a sense of 
fulfilment. 
When I talk of Jammu and Kashmir, I would say that, actually, I was 
prepared to hold the elections, both for the Lok Sabha and the Stale 
Assembly.    We could only succeeded in holding elections for Parliament.

We have the Ethics Committee. But, the atmosphere is exactly not

Assemblies of this nature. But, somehow, we could not fulfil that, and that is 
why I have been specially interested in seeing that this Ethics Committee also 
succeeds, and we are able to eliminate people, who, in fact, are not desirable. 
It may be a tall claim. But the time is going to show that our future depends on 
the kind of people, who become peoples' representatives, both in the Lok

Earlier, the time was not sufficient at my disposal because of my parliamentary

be able to work in

DR. A.R. KIDWAI (Delhi): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would like to start 
my speech with a quotation from the  President's Address. I quote, "I join all of 
you in extending hearty congratulations to our kisans who have once again 
produced a bumper crop. The output of foodgrains is projected to touch a new 
high of 210 million tonnes in 2001-02, from 196 million tonnes last year. With 
production of 81 million tonnes of milk during 2000-01, India continues to be 
the world's largest producer of dairy products. We have also made impressive 
strides in many other areas of agricultural production." 
While the average growth rate during the current year is projected to 
be 5.4 per cent, the contribution of the agricultural sector is 5.7 per cent; the 
contribution of the services sector is 6.5 per cent; but the rate of growth of 
industry has gone down to 3.3 per cent. This is most disappointing. To say that 
the low industrial growth rate and production is because of the international 
recession is partly true, but not totally true. India is the second largest market 
of the world, and if there was enough purchasing power with our farmers, with 
our people, India could have maintained its industrial growth and development 
on the basis of its own market, but I am sorry to say that we have deprived the 
farmers, we have deprived the workers of their due wages, and, that is why, in 
spite of being such a large market, it is poor; it has no purchasing capacity; it 
cannot promote any development of industry. And, therefore, economic 
policies should be given due attention. The country cannot keep on growing by 
depriving agriculture or labour of their due wages, a living wage, from their due 
profit, which they should get. If the people are poor, if the farmers are poor, if 
the workers are poor, then the country, as a whole, is poor and can never 
advance. We were expecting that the multinationals and big industries would 
come to India because of our liberalised economic policies.    They have not 
come; 
254 

[22 March. 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
and they will not come. Our strong point is that we are the second largest 
world market; but if the market is pauper, if it has no purchasing capacity, then 
how can the multinationals come? Therefore, I think, the economic policies 
require a serious relook. We have to see how we can enrich our people and 
increase their purchasing capacity. We have to improve their quality of life so 
that this rich potential can be utilised. Our agricultural production has doubled 
from 60 million tonnes to 120 million tonnes, in spite of the low productivity. 
The low productivity is because of the lack of infrastructure and because of 
the lack of inputs required for agriculture. Despite this, it is due to the hard 
labour and efforts of the farmers to improve their quality of life, that we have 
been able to achieve such a high production. So. we should utilise this 
capacity by providing them adequate infrastructure. I am glad that the Finance 
Minister, in this year's Budget, has given some emphasis and focus to 
agriculture, by reviewing the agricultural policies and by providing necessary 
funds. But, mere provision of funds does not help in the growth of agriculture 
or industry. We have been planning for a long time. Ever since the planning 
process began, we have planned in terms of money only, and set monetary 
targets. Money in the hands of the functionaries can be spent, but the 
objective will not be achieved unless -- there is also simultaneous, detailed, 
planning of the technology utilised and the procedural methods. So, the 
planning should be such that, without any difficulty, the funds can be properly 
utilised to increase production in right time and with necessary objectives. The 
planning process should consist of technological and monetary planning. That 
is why we have not been able to fulfil our targets set in our Five Year Plans, in 
our Annual Plans. We have not been able to fulfil our targets because of this 
difficulty. If we wish to make any progress in agriculture-l say this because of 
the focus-there should be a high-powered Commission set up to go into the 
technical details. Whatever money is available should be utilised to the best 
advantage to the development of agriculture. 
Regarding the empowerment of farmers to improve their conditions, 
they do not need any subsidy if they are given their due prices, due returns, 
for their work, for their production. Take the example of fixing the support 
price. The support-price-fixing formula is an uneconomic formula. It does not 
include the full cost of production, leave aside the profit. If you go on doing, 
year after year, underpricing of the foodgrains, how can the farmer prosper? 
So, there should be right pricing so that the farmer gets some advantage. If 
the farmers get rich, the country becomes rich and gets the advantage. 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2002] 
On the credit policy, the Finance Minister has proposed to increase 
the credit flow from Rs.64,000 crores to Rs.75,000 crores. What is the use of 
increasing the credit flow if, out of the Rs.64,000 crore credit flow, the farmer 
gets the advantage to the extent of only 12 per cent? How is he going to get 
more benefits out of it? Agriculture cannot afford a 16-18 per cent rate of 
interest. That is why the NABARD was established, to provide cheaper loans 
for agriculture at five per cent for those indigent people or the people below the 
poverty line; at seven per cent for the development of poultry, dairy, animal 
husbandry, fishery, for employment; and a maximum of 9.5 per cent. But the 
NABARD has no mechanism of its own of channelising its funds to the farmer. 
The funds are channelised through the commercial banks, and the commercial 
banks are lending to agriculture at the same rates as to industry, that is, 16-18 
per cent. Therefore, what is the use of the NABARD financing and the 
commercial banks refinancing? If the commercial banks lend the money at 
these high rates and "earn on the money, finance, provided by the NABARD, if 
they earn 8-10 per cent for themselves, the banks get rich, but not the farmers. 
It is a subsidy to the banks and not to the farmers. Therefore, we should 
ensure that the finances provided to the farmers are cheaper, that the 
commercial banks charge only 1.5-2 per cent of the operational costs and not 
anything extra. If the commercial banks are not willing to do that, the credit 
cooperatives can be helped to do that; the farmers' cooperatives will be the 
ideal agency for financing. Financing the farmers through the commercial 
banks at such high rates does not help them. 
Similar is the case of the fertiliser subsidy. I understand from the 
statement of the Agriculture Minister that Rs. 10,000 crores is provided as 
subsidy to fertiliser factories, in the name of agriculture. Agriculture subsidy for 
fertilisers is given to the fertiliser industry, to the tune of Rs. 10,000 crores a 
year! But some of them do not supply fertilisers at all in spite of accepting the 
subsidy. In the case of some of them who supply, the fertiliser supply, the urea 
supply, costs more than what it should. It is exploitation of the farmers. To use 
Rs. 10,000 crores a year for the technologically deficient and inefficient 
fertiliser industry, in the name of promoting agriculture, is not fair. These 
factories should improve on their own and provide fertiliser at international 
prices and utilise the subsidy for further reducing the cost of fertiliser. 
Otherwise, to go on finacning, year after year, a huge amount to the inefficient 
industry is neither good for that industry nor for agriculture. 
256 

(22 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
I had to say quite a lot of things. But, because of the shortage of 
time, I would just draw the attention of the Finance Minister to these finer 
problems. The money will be better utilised if you set up a Commission on the 
various aspects which you are going to- finance, which require improvement. 
Only then will the money be properly utilised and will we get its worth. 
Agriculture is the primary produce of this country on which the industrial 
development depends-whether it is the textile industry or the jute industry or 
the sugar industry or any other industry. And, it will remain so for times to 
come. Therefore, if you want industrial development, if you want economic 
development, if you want the development of the banks, business and 
commerce, which are all dependent on this, you have to give prime 
importance to agriculture. Unless agriculture, the primary producer of goods, 
develops, unless the farmers, the persons, who constitute 70 per cent of the 
people, who depend on agriculture, prosper, the country cannot prosper; no 
industry can prosper; and no development can take place. 
With these remarks, I hope there would be better utilisation, with the 
new focus of attention which the Finance Minister has proposed to give to 
agriculture.
